## Talk title

**Setting the legal limit with an R package: 15 years from lone scripter to open-source
regulatory infrastructure — and what changed when the AI arrived**

Shorter alternatives:

- *From SourceForge to statute: how open-source R ended up setting water quality limits in
  three countries*
- *White, grey and black: open code, confidential data, and the numbers that stop an operation*
- *I haven't written a line of code in a year: an accidental software developer's field notes*

---

## Abstract (250 words) — primary version

The sewage outfall at your local beach discharges under a licence, and so does a
produced-water stream off the North West Shelf. Both are licensed against a number: a safe
concentration for each contaminant. Exceed it and operations are modified, or stopped. That
number comes out of a species sensitivity distribution, and until recently it came out of a
closed desktop program that fitted one distribution and showed you none of its workings.

It now comes out of an R package.

I am a quantitative ecologist with a solid grasp of applied statistics and no training in
programming. This talk is the honest version of how I got from there to maintaining software
that underpins environmental regulation in Australia, New Zealand and Canada.

Three eras. First, the lone scripter: a 57-script expert-elicitation tool, published in
2012, distributed as a zip file, and unreproducible within five years. Second, packages and
GitHub — `FSSgam`, `epower`, `bayesnec`, `ssdtools` — where I discovered that `R CMD check`
is the most patient reviewer I have had, and that open code is what makes
multi-jurisdictional agreement on a method even *possible*: you cannot get three regulators
to sign off on a black box. Third, and most disorienting: I have not written a line of code
since subscribing to Claude Code, and I am roughly five times more productive.

I will be specific about where that speed-up comes from — it is not typing — and about what
has not changed. In regulatory software, someone still has to know whether the answer is
right.

*(257 words)*

---

## Abstract (150 words) — short version

I am a quantitative ecologist with no training in programming who now maintains R software
that underpins water quality regulation in Australia, New Zealand and Canada. This talk is
the honest version of how that happened.

Three eras: the lone scripter, whose 2012 published software was a 57-script zip file and
was unreproducible within five years; the package builder, who learned that `R CMD check`
is a patient reviewer and that you cannot get three regulators to agree on a black box; and
the last twelve months, in which I have not written a line of code and am roughly five
times more productive.

Along the way: `FSSgam`, `epower`, `bayesnec`, `ssdtools`, and a lot of confidential
industry data turned into public method. I will be specific about where the AI speed-up
actually comes from, and about the part of the job it cannot take.

*(148 words)*

## Speaker biography

Rebecca Fisher is a quantitative ecologist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science,
with over 25 years of experience in marine ecology and more than 100 peer-reviewed papers
and technical reports. Her interests lie at the interface between ecology, numerical
modelling and quantitative decision science, and she is committed to environmental science
research that is of direct relevance to government and industry end users.

Her recent work focuses on statistical ecotoxicology, developing robust tools for
quantifying and handling uncertainty in environmental risk management. She is an author or
contributor to the R packages `ssdtools`, `bayesnec`, `epower`, `FSSgam` and `ElicitN`, and
co-led the joint Australian–Canadian investigation that resulted in `ssdtools` being adopted
as the default software for deriving water quality guideline values.

GitHub: [beckyfisher](https://github.com/beckyfisher) ·
[open-AIMS](https://github.com/open-AIMS)

*(140 words)*
